```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyverse)
```

```{r}
#| label: load-data
# TODO (you): read the CSV and build `df`.
#
# The plots below expect `df` to have these columns:
#   CameraMaker, CameraModel, SensorDescription   (character)
#   width_mm, height_mm                           (numeric, from the "(mm)" columns)
#   width_px, height_px                           (numeric, from the "(pixels)" columns)
#   area_mm2        = width_mm * height_mm
#   megapixels      = width_px * height_px / 1e6, rounded to 2 decimal places
#   pixel_pitch_um  = width_mm / width_px * 1000
#
# Note: the original names contain parentheses, so they are non-syntactic in R.
# You need backticks around them, e.g. `SensorWidth(mm)`.

df <- read_csv("sensor_database_detailed.csv")

head(df)
```

Here is my dataset on camera sensors. We will be using this to explore how different manufacturers make products in specific sectors.

<!-- TODO: add the data source line here — where the CSV came from, with a link, plus its licence. The rubric wants this in the post itself, not only the README. -->

Let's calculate the sensor size and resolution using the data we are given. We'll use a logarithmic scale for the sensor area as the smallest sensors used are 50x smaller than the largest sensors!

We'll also calculate the pixel pitch. This is the width of a pixel and tells us how small each unit of light gathering "pixel" is. This will be interesting if a camera sensor does pixel binning or other such computational photography techniques.

```{r}
#| label: maker-groups
# TODO (you): split the makers so the busiest ones get their own colour.
#
# Produce three objects:
#   top_makers : character vector, the 7 CameraMaker values with the most rows
#   df_top     : the rows of df whose CameraMaker is in top_makers
#   df_other   : all the remaining rows

top_makers
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-sensor-area-vs-mp
#| fig-cap: "Sensor area against resolution. The seven makers with the most models are coloured; all others are grey."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
maker_colours <- c(
  "Other" = "grey80",
  setNames(scales::hue_pal()(length(top_makers)), top_makers)
)

ggplot(mapping = aes(x = area_mm2, y = megapixels)) +
  geom_point(data = df_other, aes(colour = "Other"), size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = df_top, aes(colour = CameraMaker), size = 1.4, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_number()) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = maker_colours, breaks = c("Other", top_makers)) +
  labs(
    x = "Sensor area (mm², log scale)",
    y = "Resolution (megapixels)",
    colour = "Maker"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

While we can clearly see some trends it doesn't make much sense to us right now. So let's add some calculated sensor sizes for some more context.

```{r}
#| label: sensor-formats
# TODO (you): build `formats`, a data frame of reference sensor sizes with columns
#   format    (character): '1/2.3"', '1/1.7"', '2/3"', '1"',
#                          "Micro 4/3", "APS-C", "Full frame", "Medium (GFX)"
#   width_mm  (numeric):     6.17, 7.60, 8.80, 13.20, 17.30, 23.60, 36.00, 43.80
#   height_mm (numeric):     4.55, 5.70, 6.60,  8.80, 13.00, 15.60, 24.00, 32.90
#   area_mm2  = width_mm * height_mm

formats
```

I found the sensor size data from wikipedia [here](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Image_sensor_format)

```{r}
#| label: fig-sensor-area-vs-mp-sensor-type
#| fig-cap: "Sensor area against resolution. Dashed lines mark common sensor formats. The seven makers with the most models are coloured; all others are grey."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.5
ggplot(mapping = aes(x = area_mm2, y = megapixels)) +
  geom_vline(
    data = formats, aes(xintercept = area_mm2),
    linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4, alpha = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = formats, aes(x = area_mm2, y = Inf, label = format),
    angle = 90, hjust = -0.05, vjust = 0.5, size = 2.8, inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_point(data = df_other, aes(colour = "Other"), size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = df_top, aes(colour = CameraMaker), size = 1.4, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_number()) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = maker_colours, breaks = c("Other", top_makers)) +
  labs(
    x = "Sensor area (mm², log scale)",
    y = "Resolution (megapixels)",
    colour = "Maker"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.margin = margin(t = 45, r = 5, b = 5, l = 5))
```

We notice here that there are 3 cameras with very large sensors and 3 with very small sensors so let's have a look at these.

```{r}
#| label: outliers
cols <- c(
  "CameraMaker", "CameraModel", "SensorDescription",
  "width_mm", "height_mm", "area_mm2", "megapixels"
)

# TODO (you): build `tiny` — the rows of df with area_mm2 < 10, sorted by megapixels

tiny |>
  select(all_of(cols)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Looks like it's a weird Olympus camera/music player combo along with 2 raspberry pi camera sensor modules.

Leica and Pentax medium format cameras! Very expensive.

```{r}
#| label: fig-outlier-cameras
#| fig-cap: "Look at these weirdos!"
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.5
# TODO (you): build `outliers` — the rows of `tiny` and `medium` stacked together

ggplot(mapping = aes(x = area_mm2, y = megapixels)) +
  geom_vline(
    data = formats, aes(xintercept = area_mm2),
    linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4, alpha = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = formats, aes(x = area_mm2, y = Inf, label = format),
    angle = 90, hjust = -0.05, vjust = 0.5, size = 2.8, inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_point(data = df_other, aes(colour = "Other"), size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = df_top, aes(colour = CameraMaker), size = 1.4, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_text(
    data = outliers,
    aes(
      x = area_mm2, y = megapixels, label = CameraModel,
      hjust = ifelse(area_mm2 > 100, 1.1, -0.1)
    ),
    size = 2.2, inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_number()) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = maker_colours, breaks = c("Other", top_makers)) +
  labs(
    x = "Sensor area (mm², log scale)",
    y = "Resolution (megapixels)",
    colour = "Maker"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.margin = margin(t = 45, r = 5, b = 5, l = 5))
```

We also see 2 weird dots with very high megapixel counts on comparatively small sensor sizes.

```{r}
#| label: small-high-mp
# TODO (you): build `small_high_mp` — rows of df with megapixels > 35 and area_mm2 < 200

small_high_mp |>
  select(all_of(cols)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

They turn out to be Nokia phones. These 41 mega pixel monsters were released in 2012 for the 808 and 2013 for the 1020.

They use a technique called pixel binning which takes an average of the information in adjacent pixels to make a "super pixel" that has higher low light performance.

Now that we have some weirdly dense sensors let's use the pixel pitch calculation that we did before.

```{r}
#| label: high-mp-comparison
# TODO (you): build `high_mp` — rows of df with megapixels > 35, sorted by area_mm2

high_mp |>
  select(CameraMaker, CameraModel, area_mm2, megapixels, pixel_pitch_um) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

We can see that even though the Leica S2 has a lower megapixel count than the Nokia 808, the pixel pitch ends up being over 5 times bigger. This results in better light gathering per pixel and higher image quality.
Add that to the much larger and higher quality lenses that the Leica uses and you get image quality that is incomparable to the Nokia.

The devil really is in the details!

>AI Disclosure: All analysis are my own but I used claude to give a general framework of and to pretty up graphs along with calculating the industry standard sensor sizes. For R I had claude convert the python graph code into R.
